claim: The BCP's strongest recommendation names business applications explicitly; it carves same-domain frontend+API apps out of scope; and it concedes the proxying attack cannot be prevented at application level.
quote: This architecture is strongly recommended for business applications, sensitive applications, and applications that handle personal data. [S6.1.4.3] / Note that many web applications consist of a frontend and API running on a common domain, allowing for an architecture that does not rely on OAuth 2.0. ... Such a scenario ... is not within scope of this specification. [S1]

claim: The BCP frames its architecture ranking as a security/simplicity trade-off rather than a normative requirement, and its threat model assumes XSS can defeat CSP/SRI and that malicious JS has the same privileges as application code.
quote: Each of these architectural patterns offers a different trade-off between security and simplicity. The patterns in this section are presented in decreasing order of security. [S6] / Unfortunately, history shows that even when applying these security guidelines, there remains a risk that the attacker finds a way to trigger the execution of malicious JavaScript. [S5]

claim: As of July 2026 the document is at revision -27, IESG-approved as Best Current Practice and in the RFC Editor queue with no RFC number yet assigned.
quote: The IESG has approved 'OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications' as Best Current Practice. Latest revision draft-27 (6 July 2026); RFC Editor state: RFC Ed Queue.

claim: Curity, which sells a Token Handler product, takes an absolutist position that SPAs cannot secure tokens, with no acknowledgement of acceptable browser-based OAuth cases.
quote: Currently, SPAs have no means of keeping access and refresh tokens secure from malicious code.

claim: Duende, which sells Duende.BFF for .NET, positions BFF so the browser only ever holds a session cookie and never sees access or refresh tokens.
quote: In Duende's implementation of the backend for frontend pattern, access tokens are no longer stored in the browser. The browser only ever holds a session cookie.

claim: Auth0/Okta, employer of the BCP's lead author, explicitly states that the required security level is context-dependent and that Authorization Code Flow with PKCE in a SPA may be acceptable in some contexts.
quote: The level of security required by an application depends on its specific functionality. It is the result of balancing the data confidentiality requirements with the ease of implementation. Therefore, in some contexts, using the Authorization Code Flow with PKCE and all the concerns about token management in a SPA may be acceptable. In other contexts, it is not.

claim: An independent 2026 read of the BCP prefers BFF and treats the token-mediating backend as a compromise, but never addresses same-domain or internal applications or implementation cost.
quote: Prefer BFF when you can: it provides the strongest protection against token theft and simplifies secure token lifecycle management. TMB should be only considered when a proxying BFF is impractical ... and even then, treat it as a compromise.

claim: Late-stage OAuth WG discussion of the BCP concerns cookie prefixes rather than any dissent over the architecture ranking, indicating WG consensus behind the ordering.
quote: Given that the BCP already says HttpOnly is a MUST, I'm not sure what this adds? (Neil Madden, on the __Host-Http- cookie prefix)
